title: Basal Ganglia and Neuromodulatory Neurons
intro: The basal ganglia are a set of nuclei beneath the cortex that select actions and learn from reward. Their input stage, the striatum, is made almost entirely of one cell type, the medium spiny neuron, and their learning is driven by dopamine neurons in the midbrain whose firing tracks reward prediction errors. Dopamine cells are one of several small neuromodulatory populations (with serotonin, noradrenaline and acetylcholine neurons) that broadcast state signals to the whole brain.

 Direct pathway:   dMSN ─┤ GPi/SNr ─┤ thalamus  → releases movement ('go')
 Indirect pathway: iMSN ─┤ GPe ─┤ STN → GPi/SNr → suppresses movement ('no-go')

blocks.text: The output nuclei (GPi and SNr) fire tonically and inhibit the thalamus and brainstem. The direct pathway inhibits them and so releases the selected action; the indirect pathway, through the external globus pallidus (GPe) and subthalamic nucleus (STN), increases their inhibition and suppresses competing actions (Albin, Young & Penney 1989; DeLong 1990). Dopamine excites D1-expressing direct-pathway MSNs and inhibits D2-expressing indirect-pathway MSNs, and it gates their synaptic plasticity. This classic picture is simplified: both pathways are active during movement, and they cooperate as well as compete (Cui et al. 2013).

items: Medium Spiny Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/medium-spiny): 95 per cent of striatal neurons, up and down states, D1 and D2 types, and their models.
Dopamine Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/dopamine): pacemakers whose bursts and pauses encode reward prediction errors, the link to temporal-difference learning.

Subthalamic Nucleus and Globus Pallidus Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/stn-gpe): an excitatory-inhibitory pacemaker loop, the hyperdirect brake and parkinsonian beta oscillations.
Serotonin Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/serotonin): slow raphe pacemakers linked to patience, punishment and reward discounting.
Noradrenaline Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/noradrenaline): locus coeruleus cells whose tonic and phasic modes set neural gain.

blocks.text: Other cell types in the circuit

items: Striatal fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs): PV-positive, about 1 per cent of striatal neurons, electrically coupled, providing strong feedforward inhibition onto MSNs (Koos & Tepper 1999). Modelled like cortical PV cells (Izhikevich FS; Golomb et al. 2007).

Cholinergic interneurons (TANs, tonically active neurons): large aspiny cells firing tonically at about 5 Hz that pause in response to rewarding or salient cues, in step with dopamine bursts (Aosaki et al. 1994).

GPe neurons: fast-firing GABAergic pacemakers; prototypic cells project to STN and output nuclei, arkypallidal cells project back to the striatum (Mallet et al. 2012); see Subthalamic Nucleus and Globus Pallidus Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/stn-gpe).

STN neurons: glutamatergic pacemakers with rebound bursting; the STN-GPe loop generates the beta oscillations (13 to 30 Hz) that are exaggerated in Parkinson's disease, and the target of deep brain stimulation (Terman et al. 2002 modelled this loop; see the STN and GPe page).

Other neuromodulatory neurons: serotonergic neurons of the raphe (slow, regular pacemakers, linked to patience and punishment; see Serotonin Neurons, #/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/serotonin), noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus (pacemakers whose phasic bursts signal salience and unexpected uncertainty; Aston-Jones & Cohen 2005; see Noradrenaline Neurons, #/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory/noradrenaline), and basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (attention and plasticity in cortex; the source of the cholinergic drive to cortical VIP cells).
Action selection: Gurney, Prescott and Redgrave (2001) proposed the basal ganglia as a selection mechanism and built rate models of it; Humphries, Stewart and Gurney (2006) made a spiking version.

Reinforcement learning: actor-critic models in which the striatum learns action values and dopamine provides the temporal-difference error (Houk, Adams & Barto 1995; Doya 2000); Frank (2005) built a neural network model of the direct/indirect pathways (Go/NoGo) that explains learning from positive versus negative feedback and Parkinson's disease effects.
Spiking reward learning: Izhikevich (2007) solved the distal reward problem with dopamine-modulated STDP and eligibility traces (see Reward-Modulated STDP, #/snn/learning-rules/stdp-reward).
